newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong leader meets press in ebullient form.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong leader meets press in ebullient form.

text.p: Looking relaxed and self-assured, Hong Kong's new Beijing-picked leader basked on Wednesday in a smooth handover from Britain, and declared self-rule would last into the distant future.

Torrential rain washed out a carnival parade on the final day of holiday celebrations, but Tung was ebullient as he sailed through his first news conference, bestowed honours on local worthies and played international statesman.
In his first three days in the job, Tung has successfully signalled business as usual.
A protest by up to 10,000 pro-democracy demonstrators on Tuesday passed off peacefully.
Police showed restraint even as demonstrators chanted "down with Li Peng", the Chinese premier.

The arrival of 4,000 Chinese troops backed by armoured vehicles, warships and helicopters caused hardly a ripple of concern. Some residents even welcomed the arriving People's Liberation Army troops with garlands and flowers.
And Tung has outlined a bold policy agenda to tackle everything from the astronomical price of housing to over-crowding in schools.
"I think the successful transition is a very good example to settle international issues that are left to be settled by history," Tung told the news conference.
He had been asked whether the British colonies of Gibraltar and the Falkland Islands might go Hong Kong's way.
The former shipping magnate stressed the twin themes of independence for Hong Kong -- a newly-created Special Autonomous Region of China -- and cooperation with new sovereign China.
"In terms of the short term obviously there will be conflicts and they will have to be talked through," Tung said, when asked whose side he would take if Beijing and Hong Kong interests clashed.
"But our long-term interests are very similar," he said.
He said he would like Hong Kong to become a cosmopolitan society "which combines the best of East and West". Tolerance of dissent would continue.
"I have repeated many times that demonstrations so long as they are lawful and peaceful can go right ahead," Tung said.
Beijing's pledges of "one country, two systems" and "Hong Kong people running Hong Kong" would survive for a "long, long, long, long, long time", he declared.
It became clear on Wednesday that six Hong Kong police inspectors resigned just before the handover because they feared being ordered to violate human rights.
"In view of things like the June 4 event, we don't want to serve the Special Administrative Region," former senior inspector Chik Ki-wai told Reuters.

He was referring to Beijing's bloody crackdown on the student-led Tiananmen Square demonstrations in 1989. Every year since, thousands of Hong Kong people have taken part in open-air vigils on June 4 in memory of the victims.
Chinese leaders have trumpeted the return of Hong Kong as erasing more than a century of national shame.
But on the first day of stock market trading in Shanghai on Wednesday, the euphoria ended and the hangover set in. Domestic currency class A shares in Shanghai dived by 4.11 percent to 1,253 points.
"There are no new incentives to buy after the handover," said one broker in the southern city of Shenzhen.
Hong Kong markets will pass their verdict on the post-colonial economy when they reopen on Thursday. Brokers said the only immediate cloud was Tung's comments on reining in runaway property prices.

"There are expectations that the market will rally and that Chinese money will enter the market so that it will close higher under the new flag," said Franklin Lam, director of research at SBC Warburg.
The market wound up its final trading day under British rule last Friday at a record closing high.
Business leaders expressed confidence that nothing would change under Chinese rule.
"We'll be opening for business on Thursday exactly as we closed on Friday," Hong Kong Bank chief William Purves told Cable News Network.
Economists greeted Tung's promises to make Hong Kong's economy more competitive, partly by upgrading its technological base, with some scepticism.
"This is pretty much what you'd expect for a politician coming in with a lot of promises but short on detail," said Rossiter.
"I hate to be negative, but I don't see a lot of magic behind the words."
Tung and Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen handed out honours to 12 residents.

Among those receiving the Grand Bauhinia Medal -- the equivalent of a British knighthood -- was Henry Fok Ying-tung, a business and real estate tycoon cold-shouldered for decades by the British as a communist sympathiser.
Shanghai-born Tung, 60, made a statement of his wealth to the Chief Justice of the Court of Final Appeal, Andrew Li, to comply with transparency rules affecting officials.
The declaration was not made public, but Tung said last April he had a US$47.5 million stake in his family shipping firm, Orient Overseas (International) Ltd, based on market prices at that time.
